content: In 2010, Baker D, Karalliedde L, Murray VSG, Maynard R, and Parkinson N edited the second edition of Essentials of Toxicology and Health Protection: A Handbook for Field Professionals, published by Oxford University Press in 2012. The Chemical Abstract Service (CAS) provides a registry accessible at cas.org/expertise/cascontent/registry/index.html, which was last accessed on April 16, 2020. The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation published The Global Burden of Disease: Generating Evidence, Guiding Policy, available at org/policy-report/global-burden-disease-generating-evidence-guiding-policy, also accessed on April 16, 2020. In 2012, Kreis I, Busby A, Leonardi G, Meara J, and Murray VSG edited Essentials of Environmental Epidemiology for Health Protection: A Handbook for Field Professionals, published by Oxford University Press. The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction developed the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, accessible at org/publication/sendai-framework-disaster-risk-reduction-2015-2030, accessed on April 16, 2020. Walker G, Mitchell G, Fairburn J, and Smith G authored a study titled Industrial Pollution and Social Deprivation: Evidence and Complexity in Evaluating and Responding to Environmental Inequality, published in Local Environment in 2005 (Volume 10, Issue 4, Pages 361–377). The World Health Organization (WHO) released Global Health Risks: Mortality and Burden of Disease Attributable to Selected Major Risks, available at int/iris/handle/10665/44203, accessed on April 16, 2020. WHO also published Rapid Risk Assessment of Acute Public Health Events (int/iris/handle/10665/70810) and Communicating Risk in Public Health Emergencies: A WHO Guideline for Emergency Risk Communication (ERC) Policy and Practice (int/iris/handle/10665/259807), both accessed on April 16, 2020. Additionally, WHO released Chemical Releases Caused by Natural Hazard Events and Disasters (int/iris/handle/10665/272390), accessed on the same date. The Manual for the Public Health Management of Chemical Incidents was published by WHO in 2009 (https://apps.int/iris/handle/10665/44127, accessed April 16, 2020). The Global Chemicals Outlook II: From Legacies to Innovative Solutions Synthesis Report (11822/27651/GCOII_synth.sequence=1&isAllowed=y) was also accessed on April 16, 2020. Orford R, Crabbe H, Hague C, Schaper A, and Duarte-Davidson R authored EU Alerting and Reporting Systems for Potential Chemical Public Health Threats and Hazards, published in Environment International in 2014 (Volume 72, Pages 15–25). The Joint External Evaluation Tool (JEE Tool), second edition, is available at int/iris/handle/10665/259961, accessed on April 16, 2020. Wyke-Sanders S, Brooke N, Dobney A, Baker D, and Murray V contributed to the UK Recovery Handbook for Chemical Incidents (pdf, accessed April 16, 2020). Antidotes and antivenoms are critical substances used to treat poisoning by counteracting the toxic effects of specific substances. Antidotes work by altering the kinetics or elimination of the toxic substance or by interfering with its effects at receptor sites, thereby improving patient outcomes. Antivenoms, on the other hand, are immunoglobulins that bind to and neutralize the effects of specific animal venoms, such as those from snakes or spiders. While many poisoning cases can be managed with supportive care and elimination techniques, the appropriate use of antidotes and antivenoms is essential in certain cases to rapidly improve the patient’s condition and prevent death. Their use can also reduce the medical resources required for treatment and shorten therapy duration, thereby lessening the overall burden on healthcare systems. In remote or low-resource settings where hospital services are limited, certain antidotes may be particularly important for treating poisoning. However, the availability of antidotes and antivenoms varies significantly between countries. In many lowand middle-income countries, these substances may be difficult to obtain due to lack of authorization, high costs, or limited availability in the global market. Access to antivenoms for snakebite treatment faces additional challenges, including poor regulatory frameworks, lack of manufacturing standards, inadequate research investment, poor-quality products, and insufficiently trained staff. These factors affect the availability, efficacy, and use of antivenoms, making snakebite a significant global health burden. The development of antidotes often stems from studies on the mechanisms of toxicity and the kinetics of toxic substances. Manufacturers of new drugs may also develop antidotes alongside their products, particularly for drugs requiring rapid reversal of clinical effects. The efficacy of new antidotes must be scientifically validated, initially in experimental animals and, where possible, in clinical settings. However, clinical trials for antidotes are often limited, and efficacy data may come from a combination of experimental research, biochemical studies, and clinical observations. Comprehensive scientific studies facilitate regulatory approval and registration of effective antidotes. Governments play a crucial role in ensuring the availability of antidotes and should support scientific research in this area. Registration of antidotes and antivenoms involves extensive documentation, including data on their physicochemical properties, stability, toxicity, and efficacy. However, pharmaceutical manufacturers may be reluctant to register these products due to high costs and limited market demand. Incentives such as simplified registration procedures or recognition as orphan drugs can encourage manufacturers to make antidotes more widely available. Stocking and distribution strategies should consider the frequency of use, urgency of administration, and local poisoning trends. Centralized stocking is often more practical and cost-effective, especially for expensive or infrequently used antidotes with short shelf lives. Poison centers can also coordinate emergency responses and facilitate rapid transport of antidotes to affected areas. In lowand middle-income countries, challenges such as cumbersome import procedures, economic constraints, and lack of poison centers hinder access to antidotes and antivenoms. Limited documentation of poisoning cases further complicates procurement decisions. Proper storage conditions, including temperature, light, and humidity control, are critical to maintaining the quality and efficacy of antidotes and antivenoms.
